title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

events.content:
Build and dev server both pass. Summary of changes:

- **`app/globals.css`** — Added view-transition pseudo-element rules: `.morph` for the shared-element image with a subtle blur mid-flight, `.nav-forward`/`.nav-back` for directional page slides (60px offset, asymmetric fade+slide timing), `.slide-down`/`.slide-up` for Suspense reveals, `pointer-events: none` on the transition overlay, and a `prefers-reduced-motion` block that zeroes all view-transition durations plus the existing skeleton pulse.
- **`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — Wrapped each thumbnail `<div className="product-image">` in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="morph" default="none">` and added `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}` on each `Link`.
- **`app/page.tsx`** — Wrapped the page content in a `<ViewTransition>` whose `enter`/`exit` map `nav-forward`/`nav-back` to the directional classes (with `default: 'none'` so other transitions stay put), and wrapped the Suspense fallback/content in their own `slide-down`/`slide-up` wrappers.
- **`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — Matching shared-element name on the `<div className="product-hero">`, same directional page wrapper, `nav-back` on the back link, and matching skeleton/content reveal wrappers around the details `<Suspense>`.
- **`app/react-canary.d.ts`** — `import {} from 'react/canary'` so TypeScript picks up the `ViewTransition` export that the installed `@types/react@19.1` doesn't yet include. At runtime Next.js's vendored React canary already exports it.
